IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

J U D G M E N T 
 
 
ARAVIND KUMAR, J. 
 
 
1. Heard. Leave Granted. 
2. The Appellant before this Court is the owner of a Tata Indica 
car bearing Registration No. CH -01AT-3243, which, at the 
time of the accident, bore Temporary Registration No. CH -
18(T)-80281. The said vehicle was involved in an accident on 
 
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the offending vehicle’. 

--- Page 37 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 2 of 16 
 
21.04.2013, resulting in fatal injuries to one Shri Krishan 
Singh2, who subsequently succumbed to the injuries, giving 
rise to a claim for compensation under the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988. Respondent No. 1 before this Court is the 
Insurance Company, whereas Respondent Nos. 2 to 7 were 
claimants/legal dependants of the deceased. Respondent No. 
8 was the driver of the offending vehicle at the relevant point 
of time. Respondent Nos.2 to 8 have been deleted vide Order  
of this Court  dated 19.03.202 1. In the present Appeal, the 
Appellant/Owner of the offending vehicle has assailed the 
judgment and order dated 12.12.2019 passed by the High 
Court of Delhi3, whereby the High Court, while upholding the 
compensation of Rs. 16,37,000/- awarded to the Claimants by 
the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal –1 (North), Rohini, 
Delhi4, allowed the appeal preferred by the Insurance 
Company to the extent of modifying its liability. Applying the 
principle of ‘Pay and Recover’ , the High Court directed the 
Insurance Company to satisfy the compensation awarded to 
the Claimants in the first instance, with liberty to recover the 
amount so paid from the Appellant/Owner of the offending 
vehicle, on the ground that the vehicle did not possess a valid 
 
2 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the deceased’ 
3 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the High Court’ 
4 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Tribunal’ 

--- Page 38 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 3 of 16 
 
registration certificate on the date of the accident, its 
temporary registration having expired prior thereto.  
I. BRIEF FACTS: 
3. Shorn of unnecessary details, the brief facts of the case are 
that, on 21.04.2013, at about 12:15 p.m., an accident 
occurred in front of the DTC Depot, Bawana, Delhi, 
allegedly due to the rash and negligent driving of the 
offending vehicle, resulting in th e death of Shri Krishan 
Singh, who was on his motorbike at the time . Upon 
completion of the investigation, the police filed an Accident 
Information Report (AIR) before the Motor Accident 
Claims Tribunal–1 (North), Rohini, Delhi 5, which was 
subsequently converted into Suit No. 4742 of 2016 for 
adjudication of the claim for compensation to the 
dependants of the deceased  under the Motor Vehicle Act . 
The claimants, the Insurance Company, the driver and the 
owner of the offending vehicle appeared before the Tribunal 
and filed their respective pleadings. The Insurance 
Company specifically raised a defence that, on the date of 
the accident, the driver o f the offending vehicle did not 
possess a valid driving licence and that the vehicle itself did 
not possess a valid registration certificate. 
 
5 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Tribunal’. 

--- Page 39 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 4 of 16 
 
4. The Tribunal framed three issues for consideration vide 
order dated: 11.05.2015, which are: 
1. Whether Respondent No. 3 is not liable to pay any 
compensation, driver of the offending vehicle having 
no valid driving licence at the time of the accident. 
2. Whether the petitioners are entitled to compensation, 
if yes. What amount and from whom of the 
respondents? 
3. Relief. 
 
5. Despite the specific plea raised by the Insurance Company 
that the offending vehicle did not possess a registration 
number, the Tribunal did not frame any issue in that regard. 
Instead, the Tribunal framed an issue only with respect to 
the validity of the driving licence held by the driver of the 
offending vehicle. Upon perusal of the documents produced 
by the Investigating Officer, which included a valid driving 
licence of Respondent No. 8, the driver of the offending 
vehicle, the Tribunal decided Issue No . I against the 
Insurance Company. Thereafter, upon appreciation of the 
evidence adduced by the Claimants, the Tribunal, vide 
judgment and order dated 03.10.2016, directed the 
Insurance Company to pay a sum of Rs. 16,37,000/- to the 
Claimants as compensation. 
6. Challenging the above-mentioned judgment of the Tribunal, 
the Insurance Company filed an Appeal before the High 

--- Page 40 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 5 of 16 
 
Court in MAC Appeal No. 129 of 2017 on the ground that 
the Tribunal ought to have seen that the offending vehicle 
did not have a valid permanent registration certificate which 
is not only the fundamental breach of terms of the policy but 
also the statutory mandate of Motor Vehicle Act i.e. Section 
39 of the Act. 
7. The High Court held that the offending vehicle did not 
possess valid registration on the date of the accident, i.e., 
21.04.2013, as its temporary registration had expired on 
12.04.2013. Consequently, the vehicle was being plied on a 
public road without valid registration, in breach of the terms 
and conditions of the Insurance Policy. In view of the said 
breach, the High Court held that the Insurance Company 
could not be fastened with the liability to indemnify the 
owner of the offending vehicle. Further, in  response to a 
specific query posed by the High Court as to whether the 
owner had applied to the competent authorities for an 
extension of the temporary registration, the learned counsel 
appearing for the owner answered in the negative. 
Accordingly, vide judgment and order dated 12.12.2019, the 
High Court concluded that, since the offending vehicle did 
not possess valid registration on the date of the accident, the 
liability to pay compensation ultimately rested upon its 
owner and not upon the Insurance Com pany. However, 

--- Page 41 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 6 of 16 
 
keeping in view the interests of the Claimants, the High 
Court directed the Insurance Company to satisfy the 
compensation awarded in the first instance, with liberty to 
recover the amount so paid from the owner of the offending 
vehicle. Aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order, the 
owner of the offending vehicle has preferred the present 
Appeal. 
 
II. SUBMISSION OF THE PARTIES: 
8. Shri R.K. Kapoor, learned counsel appearing for the 
Appellant/Owner of the offending vehicle, assailed the 
judgment of the High Court insofar as it permitted the 
Insurance Company to recover the compensation amount 
from the owner of the vehicle on the grou nd that its 
temporary registration had expired on the date of the 
accident. It was contended that the Insurance Company, 
having accepted the insurance premium, could not absolve 
itself of liability without establishing a specific breach of the 
terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy, particularly 
when the vehicle was subsequently registered and the 
absence of valid registration had no causal connection with 
the occurrence of the accident. It was further submitted that 
the registration of the vehicle was pending before the Motor 

--- Page 42 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 7 of 16 
 
Vehicles Department and, therefore, any delay in granting 
registration was attributable to the Registration Authority 
and not to the Appellant. Furthermore, it was contended that 
although the issue of non-registration had been raised by the 
Insurance Company before the Motor Accident Claims 
Tribunal, no specific issue in that regard was framed or 
adjudicated upon by the Tribunal. Consequently, the High 
Court ought not to have determined the said issue without 
affording the Appellant an adequate opportunity to contest 
the same. 
9. Mr. Pradeep Gaur, Learned Counsel of the 
Respondent/Insurance Company supported the High 
Court’s judgment dated 12.12.2019  by contending that the 
offending vehicle’s temporary registration had expired on 
12.04.2013, whereas the accident occurred on 21.04.2013, 
thereby violating Sections 39 and 43 of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988, as well as the insurance policy conditions. It was 
submitted that the issue of non-registration had already been 
specifically pleaded in the written statement and supported 
by evidence before the MACT, which the Appellant failed 
to rebut. Relying on Narinder Singh v. New India 
Assurance Company Limited and Others6, the Respondent 
contended that the vehicle was being driven without valid 
 
6 (2014) 9 SCC 324 

--- Page 43 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 8 of 16 
 
registration and that the High Court had rightly applied the 
principle of pay and recover, protecting the claimants while 
permitting recovery of compensation from the vehicle 
owner. Accordingly, dismissal of the Appeal was sought, as 
the impugned judgment suffered from no illegality and 
raised no substantial question of law. 
 
III. POINT FOR CONSIDERATION  
 
 
10.  Having heard the Learned Counsel for the parties and 
having considered the material available on record, the point 
that arises before this Court is as follows: 
I.  Whether the High Court was justified in directing the 
Insurance Company to pay the compensation awarded to 
the Claimants in the first instance and thereafter recover 
the same from the Appellant/Owner of the offending 
vehicle on the ground that the vehicle did not possess 
valid registration on the date of the accident?   
 
IV. ANALYSIS 
 
11. The core issue relates to offending vehicle, owned by the 
Appellant herein, was issued with  a valid temporary or 

--- Page 44 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 9 of 16 
 
permanent registration certificate on the date of the accident 
or not. 
12. The undisputed fact of the case is that on the date of the 
accident i.e. 21.04.2013, the owner of the offending vehicle 
did not have either a temporary or a permanent registration 
certificate for the vehicle. 
13. On the one hand, the learned counsel appearing for the 
Appellant contended that, on the date of the accident, an 
application seeking renewal of the registration of the 
offending vehicle was pending before the competent 
authorities and that the vehicle was subsequently granted 
permanent registration in accordance with the provisions of 
the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. It was further contended that 
the Insurance Company, having accepted the insurance 
premium, could not absolve itself of the liability to pay 
compensation. On the other hand, the learned counsel 
appearing for the Insurance Company contended that, in the 
absence of a valid registration certificate, the offending 
vehicle could not have been lawfully plied on a public road. 
It was further contended that no application seeking renewal 
or registration of the offending vehicle was pending before 
any competent authority on the date of the accident. 
14. In order to determine the correctness of the rival contentions 
advanced by the Appellant and the Respondent regarding 

--- Page 45 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 10 of 16 
 
the pendency of an application for registration before the 
competent authorities on the date of the accident, which has 
a bearing on the question of whether the offending vehicle 
possessed a valid registration certificate at the relevant point 
of time and, consequently, on the determination of liability 
as between the Insurance Company and the owner of the 
vehicle, it is necessary to examine the evidence adduced by 
the respective parties in support of their contentions. 
15. On perusal of material available on record, we find that:  
15.1. Firstly, although the Tribunal had the opportunity to 
examine the evidence relating to the aforesaid issue, it 
failed to do so, as no specific issue was framed in that 
regard, thereby depriving the parties of an opportunity 
to adduce evidence and substantiate thei r respective 
contentions on the said issue. 
15.2. Secondly, although both the contesting parties before 
this Court, namely, the owner of the offending vehicle 
and the Insurance Company, had appeared before the 
Tribunal, neither party took any steps during the 
pendency of the proceedings to seek the framing of a 
specific issue concerning the validity of the 
registration certificate of the offending vehicle, despite 
the Insurance Company having specifically pleaded 

--- Page 46 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 11 of 16 
 
that the vehicle did not possess a valid registration 
certificate on the date of the accident. 
15.3. Thirdly, the Tribunal, without determining the validity 
of the registration of the offending vehicle, proceeded 
to hold that the Insurance Company was liable to pay 
compensation merely on the ground that the driver of 
the offending vehicle possessed a valid driving licence. 
In doing so, the Tribunal failed to examine whether the 
owner of the offending vehicle had violated any of the 
terms and conditions of the Insurance Policy or the 
provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which, in 
our considered opinion, constitutes an error on the part 
of the Tribunal. 
15.4. Fourthly, the High Court, in the absence of any 
documentary evidence on record substantiating the 
plea raised by the Insurance Company that the 
offending vehicle did not possess a valid registration 
certificate on the date of the accident, proceeded to 
conclude that the vehicle was being plied without valid 
registration. The said conclusion was arrived at 
primarily on the basis of the oral response furnished by 
the learned counsel appearing for the owner of the 
offending vehicle before the High Court, without 
examining any documentary evidence or evidence 

--- Page 47 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 12 of 16 
 
adduced by the owner concerning the validity of the 
registration certificate. In our considered opinion, such 
a conclusion, in the absence of a proper examination of 
the relevant evidence, could not have been arrived at 
by the High Court. 
15.5. Fifthly, the owner of the offending vehicle did not 
adduce any evidence before the Tribunal to establish 
that an application seeking renewal of the registration 
of the offending vehicle was pending before the 
competent authorities on the date of the accident, 
although such a contention has been advanced by him 
before the High Court as well as before this Court. The 
said contention has, however, been disputed by the 
Insurance Company. Thus, despite the rival 
contentions advanced by the parties regarding the 
pendency of the application before the competent 
authorities, neither party has produced any evidence to 
substantiate its respective stand. In the absence of such 
evidence, it is not possible for this Court to arrive at a 
definitive conclusion regarding the liabili ty to pay 
compensation, as between the Insurance Company and 
the owner of the offending vehicle. 
16. For the aforesaid reasons, we are unable to arrive at a 
definitive conclusion as to who should ultimately be saddled 

--- Page 48 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 13 of 16 
 
with the liability to pay compensation, inasmuch as the 
evidence necessary for such determination is not available 
on record. The fundamental issue bearing upon the 
determination of such liability, namely, whether the 
offending vehicle possessed a valid re gistration certificate 
on the date of the accident, was neither framed nor 
adjudicated upon by the Tribunal. Even the High Court, in 
exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, did not frame the said 
issue so as to afford the parties an opportunity to adduce 
evidence in support of their respective contentions. 
Consequently, in the absence of a proper adjudication of the 
said issue on the basis of legally admissible evidence, the 
question of ultimate liability cannot be conclusively 
determined. 
17. Although the learned counsel appearing for the owner of the 
offending vehicle, in response to a specific query posed by 
the High Court as to whether the owner had applied to the 
competent authorities for an extension of the temporary 
registration, answered the same in the negative, we are of 
the considered view that, in the absence of evidence 
adduced by the respective parties on the said issue, no 
adverse inference can be drawn against the Appellant herein 
solely on the basis of such a response. 

--- Page 49 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 14 of 16 
 
18. For the aforesaid reasons, we are of the considered opinion 
that the impugned judgment of the High Court deserves to 
be set aside and the matter be remanded to the Tribunal for 
fresh adjudication of the issue concerning the validity of the 
temporary or permanent registration of the offending 
vehicle on the date of the accident. The Tribunal shall afford 
both parties an opportunity to adduce evidence in support of 
their respective contentions on the said issue, which they 
were unable to do earlier on account of the failure to frame 
a specific issue in that regard. Such a course, in our 
considered view, would safeguard the interests of both 
parties and subserve the ends of justice. 
19. The High Court, keeping in view the interests of the 
Claimants, directed the Insurance Company to pay the 
compensation awarded in the first instance, with liberty to 
recover the same from the owner of the offending vehicle. 
However, the question as to whet her the Insurance 
Company is entitled to recover the amount so paid from the 
owner shall be determined by the Tribunal upon framing the 
aforesaid issue and affording the parties an opportunity to 
adduce evidence in support of their respective contentions.  
20. For the aforesaid reasons, the Appeal is partly allowed and 
the impugned judgment and order dated 12.12.2019 passed 
by the High Court of Delhi in MAC Appeal No. 129 of 2017 

--- Page 50 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 15 of 16 
 
is hereby set aside. Consequently, Suit No. 4742 of 2016 
shall stand restored to the file of the Motor Accident Claims 
Tribunal–1 (North), Rohini, Delhi, for adjudication of the 
limited issue concerning the validity of the registration of 
the offending veh icle on the date of the accident. The 
Tribunal shall frame an appropriate issue in this regard and 
afford both the contesting parties, namely, the 
Appellant/Owner of the offending vehicle and Respondent 
No. 1/Insurance Company, an opportunity to adduce oral as 
well as documentary evidence in support of their respective 
contentions. The Tribunal shall thereafter determine 
whether the Insurance Company is entitled to recover the 
compensation amount from the Appellant/Owner of the 
offending vehicle, in accordance with law. We make it clear 
that we have not expressed any opinion on the merits of the 
aforesaid issue, and all contentions of the parties in that 
regard are left open to be urged before the Tribunal. The 
Tribunal shall adjudicate the said issue indepe ndently, on 
the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties, without 
being influenced by any observations made herein. 
However, we direct the Insurance Company to pay the 
compensation awarded by the Tribunal, along with the 
accrued interest as directed by the Tribunal, to the Claimants 
within a period of four weeks from the date of this order, if 

--- Page 51 ---
SLP (C) No.8874 of 2020  Page 16 of 16 
 
the same has not been paid already. The indemnification 
aspect would depend upon the finding that would be arrived 
at by the Tribunal by fastening the liability either on the 
insurer or the insured as the case maybe .

1. Leave granted.
2. The issue that arises in these appeals is with regard to the
time frame for determining the stamp duty payable on an
instrument, upon a reference under Section 47-A(1) of the
Indian Stamp Act, 1899. By way of the impugned judgment that
was affirmed thereafter in review, a learned Judge of the High
Court of Judicature at Madras 1, opined that the time frame of
three months mentioned in the rules was mandatory and set aside
the determination of the stamp duty payable by the respondent,
C. Vasantha, on that short ground.  Aggrieved thereby, the State
authorities are in appeal.
3. The  respondent,  C.  Vasantha,  purchased  an  extent  of
agricultural land with a farm house under registered sale deed
dated 10.06.2009. The said sale deed was referred to the
1  “High Court”, for short
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     1

--- Page 68 ---
District Revenue Officer (Stamps)2 under Section 47-A(1) of the
Indian Stamp Act, 1899, to assess whether the stamp duty paid
thereon, in terms of the market value of the property, was
accurate.  The DRO(S) issued her a notice  on 21 .08.2009 in
Form-I, under Rule 4 of the Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of
Undervaluation Of Instruments) Rules, 1968 3.  The respondent
replied thereto and the DRO(S) then issued her a notice on
11.01.2010  in  Form-II,  under  Rule  6  of  the  1968  Rules,
provisionally determining the market value of the property.
The same was confirmed by him, thereafter, by way of the final
order dated 11.02.2010, and the deficit stamp duty payable by
the respondent was determined as 3,70,272/- (Rupees three lakh₹
seventy thousand two hundred seventy two only). The appeal of
the respondent against the said order came to be dismissed by
the Inspector General of Registration on 29.11.2012.
4. Assailing these orders, the respondent approached the High
Court  by  way  of  CMA  No.  3645/2013.  By  judgment  dated
18.08.2017, a learned Judge of the High Court opined that Rule
7 of the 1968 Rules required the exercise to be completed
within three months from the date of the first notice, that is,
the notice in Form-I dated 21.08.2009 and, therefore, the final
order passed beyond 21.11.2009 was liable to be set aside on
that short ground. Further, the learned Judge noted in the
order to the effect that he did not think it necessary to go
into the merits in view of the fact that the time frame
2  “DRO(S)”, for short
3  “1968 Rules”, for short
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     2

--- Page 69 ---
prescribed under Rule 7 of the 1968 Rules had been breached by
the authorities.
5. Aggrieved by this order, the State authorities filed a review
application on 27.11.2017.  However, this review application
came to be numbered only on 24.08.2024 as Review Application
No. 232/2024. During the interregnum, this Court had occasion
to deal with the 1968 Rules and delivered its decision in
Inspector General of Registration, Tamil Nadu vs. K. Baskaran 4.
The same was relied upon by the State authorities before the
learned Judge.  However, the learned Judge refused to take note
of the said decision on the ground that it amounted to a
subsequent change in law, as it was delivered after the
judgment  was  passed  by  him  on  18.08.2017,  and  did  not
constitute a ground for review.  Stating so, the learned Judge
dismissed the review application, vide order dated 04.07.2025.
6. The judgment dated 18.08.2017 and the order dated 04.07.2025
are presently called in question.  
7. We may first note the scheme of the 1968 Rules. Rule 4 is
titled “Procedure on receipt of reference under Section 47-A”
and provides that, upon receipt of such a reference from the
registering officer, the Collector shall issue a notice in
Form-I, informing every person by whom and to every person in
whose favour the instrument has been executed, of the receipt
of the reference and asking them to submit to him their
representations, if any, in writing to show that the market
value  of  the  property  has  been  truly  set  forth  in  the
4  (2020) 14 SCC 345
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     3

--- Page 70 ---
instrument, and also to produce all evidence that they have in
support of the representation, within 21 days from the date of
service of the notice.  After considering the representations,
if any, received from the persons to whom the notice was issued
and after examining the records and evidence before him, the
Collector is to pass a provisional order, determining the
market value of the property and the duty payable. Rule 5
details the principles for determination of the market value.  
8. Rule 6 of the 1968 Rules is titled “Procedure after arriving at
provisional market value” and states that the Collector shall
communicate a copy of his provisional order, determining the
market value and the duty payable, to all the persons who are
liable to pay such duty along with a notice in Form-II and call
upon such parties to lodge their objections, if any, to such
determination of the market value within the time specified in
the notice.  The Collector is also required to hear the parties
on the date specified in the notice or on such other date, as
may be fixed by him.
9. Rule 7 is titled “Final order determining the market value”.
Sub-Rule (1) thereof is of relevance.  It reads as under: -
“(1) The Collector shall, after considering the
representations received in writing and those
urged at the time of hearing or in the absence
of  any  representation  from  the  parties
concerned or their failure to appear in person
at the time of hearing in any case after
careful  consideration  of  all  the  relevant
factors and evidence available within him pass
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     4

--- Page 71 ---
an order within three months from the date of
first notice determining the market value of
the properties and the duty payable on the
instrument, and communicate the order so passed
to the parties and take steps to collect the
difference in the amount of stamp duty, if
any.”
10. A plain reading of the aforestated Rule 7(1) makes it clear
that the time frame of three months therein is to be counted
from the date of the first notice in Form-II under Rule 6 of
the 1968 Rules. It is not relatable to the first notice in
Form-I  under  Rule  4.  This  is  apparent  as  there  is  no
determination of the market value and the duty payable at the
stage of issuance of a notice in Form-I. It is only thereafter
that the Collector is to consider the representations received
in writing and make a provisional determination. Pursuant
thereto, the Collector is to then issue the notice in Form-II
and  after  considering  the  objections  to  the  provisional
determination and upon hearing the parties, as provided in Rule
6, the Collector is to pass the final order. This exercise,
therefore, does not hinge on the notice issued in Form-I under
Rule 4, as the said notice merely culminates in a provisional
order of determination, which is then made the subject matter
of the later notice in Form-II under Rule 6 of the 1968 Rules.
The words “first notice” in Rule 7(1) only indicate that Rule 6
contemplates the possibility of more than one notice in Form-II
being issued, as the hearing of the parties may not only be on
the date specified in the first Form-II notice but may also be
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     5

--- Page 72 ---
on such other date as may be fixed by the Collector.  The
learned Judge, therefore, committed a patent error in opining
that the use of those words indicated that they were in the
context of the Form-I notice and not the Form-II notice.  
11. This aspect has been clarified by this Court in K. Baskaran
(supra).  The  said  decision  merely  clarified  the  position
obtaining under the 1968 Rules and did not bring about a change
in law, as understood by the learned Judge. Further, as rightly
noted in the aforestated decision, Rule 7 cannot be held to be
mandatory, as the time frame fixed thereunder is for the
purpose of facilitating early recovery of stamp duties, payable
to the Government, and as delay in that regard would have an
adverse impact on the exchequer. It is not to benefit a party
to a document, who is found to have under-valued the property
so as to escape the obligation of paying higher stamp duty.
That, clearly, could not have been the intention of the law
makers while fixing a time frame in Rule 7(1) of the 1968
Rules.
12. Applying  the  aforestated  principles,  we  find  that  the
adjudication by the DRO(S) of the market value, vide his final
order dated 11.02.2010, was obviously within a period of three
months, reckoned from the Form-II notice that was issued on
11.01.2010. Therefore, even on facts, there was no reason to
interfere with the said order on this inapplicable technical
ground.
13. However, as already noticed supra, the learned Judge did not go
C.As. @ SLP(C) Nos. 10522-10523/2026     6

--- Page 73 ---
into  the  merits  of  the  matter  to  verify  whether  the
determination of the market value and stamp duty was valid and
justified on facts, as the appeal was disposed of on a
technical ground.  As we find that such ground was without
legal and factual basis, the respondent would be entitled to
have her appeal decided on merits.
14. The impugned judgment dated 18.08.2017 and the order dated
04.07.2025 are, accordingly, set aside.  CMA No. 3645/2013 is
restored to the file of the High Court for consideration on
merits. The High Court shall endeavour to dispose of the appeal
in accordance with law as expeditiously as possible.
15. The appeals are allowed to the extent indicated above.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
Parties shall bear their own costs.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 1914 OF 2019 
TINKARI GHOSH                                 ….APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ANANDA MANDAL 
AND OTHERS                                     ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. The  appellant,  being  the  de-facto  complainant,  has
approached this Court by way of the instant appeal with special
leave, assailing the judgment dated 28 th April, 2016, passed by
the High Court of Calcutta1 in C.R.R. No. 1676 of 2000, whereby
the aforesaid criminal revision petition filed by the appellant
herein was dismissed.
3. The respondent herein were arraigned in an FIR No. 88 of
1992  lodged  by  the  appellant  herein  at  the  Police  Station,
Bhatar for offences punishable under Section 147, 148, 149,
341 and 325 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 2, to which Section
1  Hereinafter, referred to as “the High Court”
2  For short, “IPC”

--- Page 76 ---
2
302 IPC was subsequently added upon the death of the injured.
4. As per the FIR, ten assailants surrounded the house of the
complainant over a dispute of land of the school and took away
his brother Ekkari Ghosh and assaulted him mercilessly in the
house of the accused Satya Charan Majumdar. Injuries were
inflicted on the head and other parts of the body of the brother
of the complainant, who expired while undergoing treatment in
the Burdwan Medical College and Hospital. After investigation, a
chargesheet was filed against 17 accused persons who are the
respondents  herein.  The  trial  Court  framed  charges  under
Sections  304/34  and  342/34  against  the  respondents  who
pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.  Upon conclusion of trial,
the  trial  Court  proceeded  to  acquit  the  respondents  of  the
charges vide judgment dated 16 th June, 2000 by extending the
benefit of doubt to the respondents.
5. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment of the
trial  Court,  the  appellant  herein,  being  the  de-facto
complainant, filed the aforesaid revision petition before the High
Court, which came to be dismissed by the judgment dated 28 th
April, 2016 which is subject matter of challenge in this appeal
with special leave.
6. We have heard and considered the submissions advanced
by  Mr.  Ranjan  Mukherjee,  learned  AOR  representing  the
appellant  and  Mr.  Rauf  Rahim,  learned  senior  Advocate,
representing  the  respondents,  and  have  gone  through  the

--- Page 77 ---
3
judgments rendered by the trial Court and the High Court, as
also other material placed on record.
7. We  find  grave  discrepancies  in  the  testimony  of  the
material prosecution witness, namely, Tinkari Ghosh (PW-1),
the appellant herein, and Anil Ghosh (PW-2), and so also grave
contradictions  inter  se in  the  testimony  of  the  so-called
eyewitnesses and of Dr. Pradip Kumar Ghosh, Medical Jurist
(PW-13).
8. The number of accused named in the FIR was 10, whereas
at the trial, the said number was increased to 17 by the alleged
eye-witnesses while deposing at the trial.
9. On a perusal of the statement of Tinkari Ghosh (PW-1), the
appellant herein, it becomes clear that he stated about two sets
of incidents which took place on 7 th August, 1992. In the first
set,  the  accused  persons,  17  in  number,  pelted  stones  and
brickbats at his house. Thereafter, some members of the school
committee,  who  had  come  to  his  house,  managed  to  flee
through the back door. The accused persons turned their wrath
towards these members, one of which was Ekkari Ghosh, the
brother of the complainant.
10. The  complainant  alleged  that,  after  two  hours  Shanti
Ghosh and Anil Ghosh came to his house and reported that
Ekkari  Ghosh  had  been  forcefully  confined  by  the  accused
persons at the RI office and was being brutally assaulted. When
the complainant reached the RI office, he saw Ekkari Ghosh

--- Page 78 ---
4
lying  unconscious  inside  the  Bhangagara  Club/RI  office.
Apparently thus, Tinkari Ghosh (PW-1) was not an eyewitness
to the alleged assault made on Ekkari Ghosh and his evidence
regarding the second incident is hearsay.
11. Anil  Ghosh  (PW-2) stated that  as many  as 17 accused
persons  assaulted  Ekkari  Ghosh  on  his  head.  As  a  result,
Ekkari Ghosh fell down and the accused continued to strike
him with lathis, iron rods, etc. Thereafter, the accused dragged
Ekkari Ghosh to the house of Satya Charan Majumdar. From
there, the Ekkari Ghosh was taken to Bhangagar Club/RI office.
After this, the witnesses Anil Ghosh and Satya Ghosh reported
the incident to the complainant. Similar evidence was given by
Shanti Ghosh (PW-3), though of course, with a divergent figure
regarding the number of the assailants.
12. Dr. Pradip Kr. Ghosh, (PW-13), Medical Jurist, stated that
he  conducted  post-mortem  and  observed  11  ante-mortem
injuries on the body of the Ekkari Ghosh while conducting the
autopsy.  However, while deposing, the Doctor failed to give any
details whatsoever of the injuries noted by him in the post-
mortem report. 
13. Although the Doctor opined that the death was homicidal
in nature, he did not state that any head injury was noted on
the body of the deceased. He also did not state that any of the
injuries, either individually or cumulatively, was sufficient in
ordinary course of nature to cause death.

--- Page 79 ---
5
14. In this background, we are of the opinion that the evidence
of the prosecution witnesses is full of material contradictions
and discrepancies.
15. The  trial  Court,  upon  appreciation  of  the  evidence  on
record, inter alia, arrived at a conclusion that the very presence
of the purported eyewitnesses at the place of occurrence was
doubtful and that their testimonies were inconsistent with the
allegations made in the FIR and with each other on material
particulars  relating  to  the  place  of  incident  and  manner  of
occurrence. In this background, the trial Court concluded that
the prosecution had failed to establish the guilt of the accused
beyond reasonable doubt and accordingly acquitted them by a
well-reasoned judgment dated 16th June, 2000.  
16. The High Court, while considering  the  challenge to the
order  of  acquittal  in  the  revision  filed  by  the  complainant
observed that it was not the case of the revisionist that the trial
Court had excluded any material evidence from consideration or
overlooked any evidence which could have a decisive bearing on
the outcome of the case. Finding no miscarriage of justice or
perversity  in  the  judgment  of  acquittal,  the  High  Court
dismissed the revision petition and affirmed the acquittal.
17. This Court, while examining a challenge to the concurrent
findings of fact recorded in favour of the respondents being the
acquitted  accused  persons,  would  be  loath  to  interfere  with
such findings unless any perversity or gross illegality is pointed

--- Page 80 ---
6
out in the impugned judgments. No such perversity has been
demonstrated before us.
18. Law is well-settled by a catena of decisions of this Court
that, while considering an appeal against acquittal, the Court
should be slow to interfere where two views are possible, and
the view in favour of the accused should be given primacy. 
19. In this background, we find no merit in this appeal, which
is accordingly dismissed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No.     /2026
(Arising out of SLP(Crl.)  No.13390/2026)
VIKRAM                                  Appellant
                      VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA                        Respondent
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  has  challenged  the  impugned  judgment
and  order  dated  21.05.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court
Punjab and Haryana in CRMM No. 16006/2026 whereunder
the appellant prayed for grant of regular bail and same has
been dismissed.
4. It is the case of the prosecution that appellant and his
family members continuously harassed the deceased for a
   SLP(Crl.)  No.13390/2026         Page   1   out of 4

--- Page 95 ---
Creta  Car  and  a  Gold  Chain,  denied  her  food  during
pregnancy and secretly administered abortion pills causing
her  miscarriage  which  ultimately  led  to  her  to  commit
suicide on 16.03.2025.
5. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.  Mr.  K  Parameshwar,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant submits that medical records
conclusively prove that deceased was suffering from pre-
existing ailments Brain TB, PCOD, Kidney Stones and her
pregnancy was not viable (missed abortion) leading to a
medically advised (D&C) procedure on 15.03.2025 and she
was  never  administered  or  forced  to  consume  abortion
pills. He also contends that appellant was a caring husband
who  constantly  provided  the  deceased-wife  the  medical
treatment  and  had  in  fact  admitted  the  deceased  to
medical insurance in the month of February, 2025, which
contradicts the prosecution theory of cruelty and denial of
food and care. Hence, he prays for allowing the appeal
grant of bail. Whereas, the learned counsel appearing for
the  respondent-State  supports  the  impugned  order  and
prays for dismissal of the appeal.
   SLP(Crl.)  No.13390/2026         Page   2   out of 4

--- Page 96 ---
6. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties, we notice at the outset, that there is a delay of 18
hours in registering the FIR. The initial statement given by
the brother of the deceased during the inquest proceedings
does not contain any allegation of dowry demand cruetly or
suspicion  against  the  appellant.  Prima  Facie,  the  post
mortem  report  also  indicate  that  the  dead  body  of  the
deceased as found was healthy with no external injury or
struggle marks and as such the prosecution will have to
establish  beyond  reasonable  doubt  the  alleged  physical
assault and starvation meted out to the deceased. Hence,
we desist from examining the grounds urged in the present
appeal as it is likely to prejudice the prosecution case.
7. For the reasons aforesaid, we are of the considered
view  that  appellant  is  entitled  to  be  released  on  bail.
Accordingly, we allow this appeal is allowed and set aside
the impugned order. Appellant is ordered to be released on
regular  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional Court deems fit to impose.
   SLP(Crl.)  No.13390/2026         Page   3   out of 4

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO(S).17534 OF 2026)
NAVAGYOTH                                     APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF KERALA & ANR.                        RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the order dated 08.09.2026
passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in
Bail Application No. 4860 of 2026. 
This  criminal  appeal  arises  out  of  crime
registered pursuant to FIR No. 1270 of 2026 dated
22.07.2026 lodged with PS Kodungalloor, District
Thrissur Rural, for the offences punishable under
Sections  69  and  318(4)  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023. Anticipating arrest in connection
with  this  crime,  the  appellant  preferred  Bail
Application No. 4860 of 2026 before the High Court
of Kerala at Ernakulam seeking anticipatory bail.
By impugned order dated 08.09.2026, the High
Court dismissed the application for anticipatory
bail. Hence, the present appeal. 
1

--- Page 113 ---
By order dated 17.09.2026, this Court issued
notice in the instant matter, while granting interim
protection from arrest to the appellant. 
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
in support of the appeal and learned counsel for the
respondent(s)-State.
Learned counsel for the appellant contended that
FIR  NO.1270  of  2026  dated  22.07.2026  at  PS
Kodungalloor, District Thrissur Rural, is a false
and frivolous complaint that has been made against
the appellant herein; though there were talks of
marriage and the marriage in fact was to take place,
there were certain disputes which arose between the
families which did not result in the parties coming
together  in  matrimony.  Hence,  the  complainant
invoked Sections 69 and 318(4) of the BNS. The
allegations against the appellant herein are wholly
false as there was complete consent on the part of
the so-called victim and in fact the parties were to
be married. In the circumstances, this Court may set
side the impugned order by making the interim order
dated 17.09.2026 absolute.
Per contra , learned standing counsel for the
2

--- Page 114 ---
respondent(s)-State with reference to his counter-
affidavit  contended  that  the  complainant  has
suffered  owing  to  the  acts  of  commission  and
omission on the part of the appellant herein; that
in fact the appellant had also retained the gold
ring which was given by the complainant to the
appellant; that having promised that he would get
married to the complainant, he has declined to do so
and hence, the complainant was constrained to invoke
Sections 69 and 318(4) of the BNS. He submitted that
the  appellant  has  employed  deceitful  means  and
hence, there is no merit in this appeal.
Considering the circumstances on record, in our
view, the appellant is entitled to the relief of
anticipatory bail sought.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set aside
the order passed by the High Court of Kerala at
Ernakulam dated 08.09.2026. 
We direct that in the event of arrest of the
appellant, the Arresting Officer shall release the
appellant  on  bail,  subject  to  furnishing  cash
security in the sum of Rs.25,000/- (Rupees Twenty-
Five Thousand only) with two like sureties.
3

--- Page 115 ---
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation/
trial, if any.
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and
shall not in any way influence the witnesses or
tamper with the material on record.
With  the  aforesaid  directions,  the  criminal
appeal is allowed.

This appeal challenges the order dated 10.12.2025
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in

Apprehending  arrest  in  connection  with  crime

Samastipur in respect of the offences punishable under
Sections  30(a),  41(1)(2)  and  47  of  the  Bihar
Prohibition  and  Excise  Act,  2016,  the  appellant
preferred an application before the High Court seeking
anticipatory  bail  in  terms  of  Section  482  of  the
1

--- Page 119 ---
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023(“BNSS” for
short).
The application for anticipatory bail having been
rejected by the High Court  vide the impugned order
dated  10.12.2025,  the  instant  appeal  has  been
preferred.
By order dated 24.03.2026, this Court passed the
following order: 
“Delay condoned. 
Issue notice to the respondent, returnable on
27.04.2026. 
Mr.Prem Prakash, learned counsel accepts notice
on behalf of the respondent.

steps shall be taken as against the petitioner
herein in relation to FIR No.5133021210205/2021
dated  28.08.2021  registered  at  Police  Station-
Khanpur,  District  Samastipur  subject  to  the
petitioner co-operating with the investigation.”
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent/State. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that  FIR
No.5133021210205/2021 dated 28.08.2021 registered at

include the name of the appellant herein. Further, the
appellant herein was neither the owner nor the driver of

--- Page 120 ---

counsel for the appellant further submitted that by order
dated  24.03.2026,  this  Court  has  granted  interim

granted by this Court may be made absolute.
Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent/State
with reference to his counter affidavit submitted that
there  is  no  merit  in  this  appeal.  He  however,  also

Considering the circumstances on record, in our

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant who has been arraigned as an accused in
FIR  No.56/2025  registered  at  Police  Station  Chhawni,
District  Durg  (C.G.)  for  the  offence  punishable  under
Section  21(C)  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Pyschotropic
Substances  Act,  1985  (for  short  “NDPS”)  is  seeking  for
being enlarged on bail.
4. On  01.02.2025  the  jurisdictional  police  received  a
secret information that appellant along with other persons
selling narcotics tablets near Baikunthdha, Podium using a
Pulsar motorcycle. The police accordingly, conducted a raid
SLP (Crl.)  No.10667/2026             Page   1   out of3

--- Page 124 ---
and  recovered  four  boxes  containing  8  strips  each  of
Alprazolam tablet, total 1200 tablets from the possession of
the appellant. The prosecution alleges that the contraband
was recovered from his possession constituted commercial
quantity under the NDPS Act.
5.  We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
contends  that  vehicle  was  seized  by  the  police  in
connection with Crime No. 56/2025 registered at Chhawni
Police Station, the appellant being the registered owner of
the seized motorcyle.  It is contended that the mandatory
procedural safeguards contemplated under Section 42 and
50 of NDPS Act was not complied with during search and
seizure. It is also contended that no independent witnesses
were associated during the recovery from a public place
rendering the prosecution case doubtful. Hence, appellant
seeks for being enlarged on bail.
6. Per  contra,  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-State submit that contraband was seized from
the conscious possession of the appellant and, as such, he
is not entitled for the discretionary relief at the hands of
SLP (Crl.)  No.10667/2026             Page   2   out of3

--- Page 125 ---
this Court.
7. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties  and  on  perusal  of  the  records,  we  notice  that
appellant has no criminal antecedents and chargesheet has
been filed and trial is in progress. Hence, we are of the
considered view that appellant is entitled to be released on
bail.  The  fact  that  the  appellant  is  in  custody  from
01.02.2025 would also persuade us to grant the prayer
sought for. Hence, appeal is allowed, impugned order is set
aside and appellant is ordered to be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Court deems
fit to impose.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.16721 OF 2026)
MAAZ KHAN  ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant who has been arraigned as an accused in FIR No. 53/2026 for
the offences punishable under Sections 25 and 27 of Arms Act, Section
5(1)/6 of POCSO Act, Section 66(E) of IT Act, Sections 3 and 5 of M.P .
Freedom of Religion Act, Sections 238(a), 3(5), 308(5), 351(2) 64(2)(m),
65(1), 78(1)(ii)(iii) of BNS, 2023, is seeking for grant of bail.
4. The gist of the prosecution case is that prosecutrix went out with co-
accused Osaf Ali Khan, who allegedly stopped the car at a secluded place
and  had  forceful  sexual  intercourse  with  her.  She  has  alleged  that
thereafter he threatened her and stated that he would marry her if she
adopted his religion and repeatedly committed rape on her under the
threat of making video, that has been recorded, viral. It is also alleged by
her  that  he  demanded  Rs.1,00,000/-  (Rupees  One  Lakh)  and  she
purportedly said to have paid Rs.40,000/- (Rupees Forty Thousand). Other
1                                                                                   SLP(CRL.) NO.16721 OF 2026

--- Page 129 ---
principle  contentions  of  the  prosecution  is  that  appellant  was
accompanying  the  principal  accused and had  given his  mobile  to the
accused.
5. On the basis of the supplementary statement recorded on 03.02.2026,
after  the  period of  almost 10 months  from the  date  of first incident,
alleging that vehicle was provided to prime accused and the video had
been  recorded  by  the  appellant,  as  informed  by  Osaf  Ali  Khan  (Co-
accused), appellant came to be arraigned as an accused.
6.  Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the records, we notice that undisputedly the appellant was not
the perpetrator of committing the rape on the prosecutrix. That apart,
during the first statement which was recorded before the jurisdictional
magistrate, she has not implicated the appellant. It is for the prosecution
to establish during the course of the trial as to what was the complicity of
the  appellant  based  on  the  further  statements  said  to  have  been
furnished by her. Hence, at this stage, we are of the considered view that
continued incarceration of the appellant is not warranted.
7. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered  to  be  released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional court may deem fit to impose.
8. It is made explicitly clear that trial court shall not be influenced by any
of the observations made hereinabove and this order shall in no way
enure to the benefit of the prime accused Osaf Ali Khan.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Criminal Appeal No(s).   /2026
@ SLP (Crl.) No(s).12844/2026
MOHAMMED ASGAR                                     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF KARNATAKA                                 Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 03.03.2023 passed by
the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru dismissing the revision of
the  appellant  against  the  order  of  the  learned  Magistrate
convicting  and  sentencing  him  for  offences  punishable  under
Sections 279, 337 and 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and
awarding sentence of six months of imprisonment along with fine.
4. The  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that  the
appellant is a roadways bus driver; the victim was riding a
scooter; in the accident, the victim sustained grievous injuries
resulting in his death. It is submitted that the appellant by now
has already served about two months of sentence; his family would
suffer if he is incarcerated for long. Therefore, ends of justice
would be served if the sentence is reduced to the period of
sentence already undergone by the appellant.
1

--- Page 143 ---
5. Having regard to the facts of the case, we are of the view
that ends of justice would be served if the period of sentence is
reduced  to  the  period  of  sentence  already  undergone  by  the
appellant.
6. The appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms. The
order impugned stands modified to the extent indicated above. The
appellant who is on bail need not surrender. His bail bonds shall
stand discharged. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

4. On the necessity for clarification, on behalf of the applicant

compensation is to be considered. According to the applicant, this
confusion has arisen on account of a confusing statement in the
order dated 18.11.2014 wherein, while disposing of the appeals,
this Court had observed:
“Having heard learned counsel for the parties,
we  are  of  the  view  that  while  coming  to
conclusion that no case is made out to direct
specific performance of contract but to award
compensation, the quantum should be arrived at
based on certain factors such as the amount for
which  the  contract  for  the  agreement  was
reached between the parties, the number of
years  passed  in  the  meantime,  who  was
responsible for such delay etc...” 
(Emphasis supplied)
7. It has been urged that the High Court had not denied specific
performance  of  the  contract  rather  the  decree  of  specific
performance was affirmed; only to balance the equities, the High
Court had enhanced the compensation payable to the respondent and,
therefore,  the  following  observation:  “while  coming  to  the
conclusion that no case had been made out to direct for specific
performance  of  contract”  is  incorrect  in  the  order  dated
18.11.2014, and the same is being wrongly interpreted by the other
side to seek eviction of the applicant from the premises by serving
a notice upon the applicant, and filing a writ petition for

by Parents, hence these countries (100 plus including U.S.A.)

2. Earlier,  after  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the

Highways Act, 1956 (published on 3 rd June, 2005), there
was no description of the nature/category of the land.
Whereas, in the Notification dated 27th April, 2006 issued
under Section 3D of the Act (appended with the petition)

petitioner that since the notification under Section 3D
was  issued within  a year  of the  Notification under

development that had come into being in the interregnum.
Learned counsel was not able to clarify this position.

have  concluded  against  the  petitioner  and  the  total
compensation  payable would  only be  in the  range of

order which is set out hereinbelow:

made  by  the  learned  counsel  for  the

surely be a reasoned one, and communicate the
same  to  the  bidders/petitioners.  It  goes
without saying, any bidder aggrieved by the
decision shall be at liberty to seek such
remedy as available in law.  The petitions
along  with  the  pending  applications  are,
accordingly, disposed of. No costs.”
Needless to observe that the petitioner(s) will

O R D E R
The petitioner stands convicted for
the offences punishable under Sections
302, 201 and 34 of IPC and 27 (1) of the
Arms Act. 
The  Criminal  Appeal  No.734/2025
filed  by  the  petitioner  is  pending
hearing before the High Court of Orissa
at Cuttack. 
While considering the application
for  suspension  of  sentence  being  IA
No.1623/2025, the High Court vide the
impugned order dated 15.07.2026 granted
three  months  interim  suspension  of
sentence to the petitioner which expired
on 22.10.2026.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                 OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.14980 OF 2026)
TINKU KUMAR @ PRABHU KUMAR @ PRABHU
CHAUDHARY
..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. On 19.01.2025 at about 9:15 pm, 9-10 armed persons are said to have
entered the E-cart logistics office (Khabra Branch), where the informant’s
brother Prakash Kumar was working as a delivery boy and the assailants
are  said to have held and stabbed the hostages, assaulted them and
looted approximately Rs.4,95,000/- from cash counter along with mobile
phones. While taking the money, the office sirens seems to have rung,
promptly  one  of  the  assailants  shot  Prakash  Kumar,  which  resulted
ultimately in his death. Hence, FIR No. 33/2025 was registered at Police
Station  Muzaffarpur  Sadar  against  9-10  unknown  persons.  During  the
course of the investigation, based on the confessional statement of co-
accused Sandeep Jha, Raja Babu, Nitesh Kumar and Vishun Kumar Sah, the
appellant  was  apprehended  and  supplementary  charge-sheet was  filed
against him. Subsequently the charges have also been framed.
1                                                                               SLP(CRL.) NO.14980 OF 2026

--- Page 227 ---
4.  Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the records, it would emerge therefrom that the co accused
Mohit, Nitesh Kumar, Abhishek Kumar, Sandeep Kumar Jha and all others
have been granted bail. Undisputedly, the appellant was not named in the
FIR. His involvement surfaced during the confessional statement of the co-
accused (referred to herein supra). There has been no recovery made from
his possession. Having regard to the fact that co-accused who are similarly
placed, as that of the appellant herein, having been granted bail, we are of
the considered view that appellant is also entitled for grant of regular bail
on ground of parity.
5. Hence, the appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and conditions as the
jurisdictional court may deem fit to impose.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Heard Mr. Mukul Rohtagi, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the petitioner.
The petitioner approached the High Court by way of Criminal
Revision Application No. 298/2005, seeking quashing of the order

--- Page 271 ---
2
passed by the trial Court, whereby the discharge application
preferred by the petitioner seeking discharge from the offence
punishable under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, was
rejected.
The case set up by the prosecution is that the petitioner and
the deceased were engaged to each other, but thereafter, the
relationship came under strain. The deceased was demanding the
papers relating to the divorce allegedly obtained by the petitioner
from his earlier marital relationship. It is alleged that the
petitioner  refused  to  supply  the  said  papers.  The  deceased
committed suicide at her residence on 29.07.2004. The FIR came to
be lodged on 30.09.2004.
Mr.  Rohatgi,  learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner, submits that there is no material whatsoever on record
to show that the petitioner by any act or omission instigated the
deceased to commit suicide. 
Issue notice.
List on 23.11.2026.
In the meantime, further proceedings in Sessions Case No.
244/2005, arising out of C.R.No.271/2004, registered at Versova
Police Station, Mumbai, shall remain stayed.

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) Diary No(s). 62029/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  27-02-2026
in CRLMC No. 274/2026 passed by the High Court of Orissa at 
Cuttack]
LAGNAJIT PATTANAYAK & ORS.                         Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA & ANR.                             Respondent(s)
IA No. 323377/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING
IA No. 323383/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 26-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANDEEP MEHTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DEVENDRA KUMAR UPADHYAYA
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. S Debabrata Reddy, Adv.
                   Mr. Ramendra Mohan Patnaik, AOR
                   
                   
For Respondent(s)  
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the petitioners.
Delay condoned.
The  petitioners  are  facing  trial  for  various  offences
including the offence punishable under Section 4 of the Protection
of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short, ‘POCSO
Act’). 
The contention advanced on behalf of the petitioners is that
the matriculation certificate of the victim was permitted to be
exhibited by the trial Court on 09.12.2005, at the stage of final

--- Page 277 ---
2
arguments.
At that point of time, the petitioners-accused moved an
application seeking production of the Birth Register of the year
1993, maintained at the Community Health Centre (C.H.C.), Betnoti,
Mayurbhanj, Odisha and summoning of the concerned Medical Officer,
C.H.C., Betnoti, to establish their defence that there was a
discrepancy  between  the  actual  date  of  birth  of  the
victim/prosecutrix and the date recorded in the matriculation
certificate.
The trial Court rejected the said application, and the High
Court also declined to interfere with the said order.
Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioners  submits  that  the
discrepancy in the Date of Birth, if proved, would be a vital
defence material in favour of the accused. It is, therefore,
contended  that  summoning  of  the  relevant  records  showing
contemporaneous entries of Date of Birth of the victim, along with
the relevant witness, is absolutely essential for a just decision
of the case, more particularly when the prosecution was allowed to
exhibit the matriculation certificate, at the stage of final
arguments.
The matter requires consideration. Issue notice.
List on 14.12.2026.
In the meantime, further proceedings in G.R.Case No. 1430/2013
pending before the Court of the learned Special Judge under the
POCSO Act, Mayurbhanj, Baripada, Odisha, shall remain stayed. 
(VARSHA MENDIRATTA)                         (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

                    Mr. Zeeshan Ali, Adv.
                    Mr. Amit Panday, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Petitioners  were  the  claimants  before  the  Motor
Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) seeking compensation for
the death of the deceased who was a cleaner and helper in
an Eicher Tempo. MACT awarded total compensation of
19,29,760/- (Rupees Nineteen Lakh Twenty Nine Thousand₹
Seven Hundred and Sixty Rupees Only). This award was
assailed by the first respondent before the High Court of
Gujarat  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter).
1

--- Page 345 ---
Petitioners did not file any appeal before the High Court
seeking enhancement of compensation.
3. By the impugned order dated 28.01.2026, High Court
dismissed the appeal preferred by the first respondent.
4. In  Special  Leave  Petition  before  this  Court,
petitioners seek enhancement.
5. We are of the view that petitioners, if aggrieved,
ought to have sought for enhanced compensation before the
High Court. Having not done that, it is not permissible
for the petitioners to approach this Court in Special
Leave Petition seeking enhancement.
6. In  the  circumstances,  we  grant  liberty  to  the
petitioners  to  approach  the  High  Court  by  filing
appropriate  appeal  seeking  enhancement  of  the
compensation awarded by the MACT. If such an appeal is
filed within a period of six weeks form today, the same
shall be entertained and considered by the High Court on
its own merits.
7. Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

--- Page 447 ---
2
2. Learned  counsel  for  the  applicant/appellant  has
argued before this Court that, in spite of his best
efforts, the matter has not been finally heard and that,
since the applicant/appellant has undergone more than seven
years of imprisonment, the application for suspension of
sentence may be allowed.

and learned Amicus Curiae appearing for respondent No.2–
complainant  have  vehemently  opposed  the  prayer  for

counsel for the parties, perusing the record, and keeping
in view the period of incarceration undergone by the
applicant/appellant, is of the opinion that the application
for  suspension  of  sentence  deserves  to  be  allowed.
Accordingly, the application is allowed.

be released on bail during the pendency of the appeal,
subject to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the Trial Court.

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 1920/2025
MOHD. SADIQ                                        Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
TRILOK SINGH RAWAT & ANR.                          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1.  The Petitioner seeks transfer of the industrial dispute case
filed by him before the Presiding Officer, Labour Court/ Industrial
Court,  Haldwani,  Uttarakhand  to  the  Presiding  Officer,  Labour
Court/Industrial Court, Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir.
2. The petitioner has contended that since he is a poor labourer
and residing in Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir, the proceedings should be
transferred there.
3. We are of the opinion that simply because the petitioner is
residing  in  Reasi,  that  cannot  be  a  ground  to  transfer  the
proceedings from the Industrial Court, Haldwani, Uttarakhand to the
Industrial Court, Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir. 
4. However, the petitioner would be at liberty to seek hearing by
virtual mode, if such facility is available in the Court of Reasi,
Jammu & Kashmir or to be represented by a counsel, as may be
desirable.
5. The Transfer Petition is dismissed with the above observations.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
…………………………………………………………………. J.
(SANDEEP MEHTA)
New Delhi,
12th AUGUST, 2026
